section_summary: These pages trace State Department, Army, Labor Department, and Far Eastern Commission disagreements over union rights for Japanese government workers and the National Public Service Law. Later documents assess Communist influence in Japanese unions, proposed changes to labor legislation, and a possible American labor mission. The section also contains a brief exchange about Japanese technicians working in China and observations on labor in Korea and Okinawa.

subfiles.title: Applicability of FEC O45/5 to Japanese Government Workers
subfiles.about: Sets out the Department’s qualified view that FEC trade union principles apply to Japanese government employees.
subfiles.summary: Distinguishes strike, bargaining, and organizing rights by category of government employee and urges avoiding public controversy over the U.S. interpretation.

subfiles.title: SCAP’s Labor Position
subfiles.about: Recommends an urgent interim directive granting most Japanese government workers organizing and bargaining rights without strike rights.
subfiles.summary: The authors argue that SCAP’s proposed restrictions would harm democratic unions, aid Communist propaganda, and alienate Commonwealth governments, the U.S. Labor Department, and American labor organizations.

subfiles.title: SCAP’s Labor Position
subfiles.about: Revises the proposal for an interim directive on union rights for Japanese government workers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum supports organizing and bargaining rights for nonadministrative government employees while withholding strike rights. It cites domestic Japanese conditions, FEC ambiguity, Commonwealth concerns, and U.S. labor opposition to SCAP’s approach. It suggests asking SCAP whether he prefers a formal directive or administrative advice.

subfiles.title: The Application of JC Serial Number 63 to Japanese Government Employees
subfiles.about: Examines whether “Japanese workers” in JC Serial Number 63 includes government employees.
subfiles.summary: Snow traces the directive’s drafting history from SWNCC and FEC papers and concludes that its framers intended at least some government employees, including transport and communications workers, to be covered.

subfiles.title: Points at Issue Between General MacArthur and State-Labor-Army on Japanese Governmental Labor
subfiles.about: Compares MacArthur’s and State-Labor-Army’s positions on strikes, union representation, and collective bargaining.
subfiles.summary: State-Labor-Army favors an occupation-period strike ban, freely chosen representatives, and broader bargaining and arbitration rights for industrial government workers than MacArthur proposes.

subfiles.title: Japanese Employment Abroad
subfiles.about: Records China’s explanation for seeking permission to employ Japanese technicians at a restored Canton paper mill.
subfiles.summary: Tsui says the proposed technicians are tied to restitution of the looted mill and do not change China’s general policy on Japanese travel.

subfiles.title: Draft Radio to SCAP on the National Public Service Law
subfiles.about: Objects to proposed U.S. instructions requiring changes to Japan’s draft National Public Service Law.
subfiles.summary: Green argues that changing Article 98 could undo a Japanese political compromise, delay legislation, and shift responsibility for resulting labor unrest from SCAP to Washington.

subfiles.title: Labor Policy in Japan
subfiles.about: Records an October 21 interoffice meeting on U.S. policy toward Japanese government workers’ labor rights.
subfiles.summary: Participants agree broadly on desirable union rights but differ over directing SCAP against his judgment. Saltzman proposes reaffirming U.S. preferences while accepting SCAP’s assessment of current conditions. Legal officers maintain that FEC policy covered some government workers, and Sullivan warns of objections from Labor, unions, and FEC members.

subfiles.title: Soviet Press Report on Japanese Labor Policy
subfiles.about: Reports Soviet press coverage of Derevyanko’s protest to MacArthur over Japanese labor policy.
subfiles.summary: The Soviet press quoted and summarized Derevyanko’s November 12 letter protesting Japanese government and occupation labor policy.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Commission Handling of the National Public Service Law
subfiles.about: Reviews possible FEC action following a British statement on Japanese public service legislation.
subfiles.summary: Claxton warns that a Soviet or Commonwealth proposal expanding government workers’ rights might win broad FEC support and place the United States in a minority. He urges a U.S. decision before the Commission’s next meeting.

subfiles.title: Labor Policy in Japan
subfiles.about: Requests urgent Army review of a proposed U.S. reply to New Zealand’s FEC questions on Japanese labor policy.
subfiles.summary: Ray asks Reid to seek the Army Secretary’s approval or comments before the January 13 Commission meeting.

subfiles.title: Labor Policy in Japan (FEC-045/5 et al.)
subfiles.to: United States member of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Drafts a response to New Zealand’s questions about FEC labor policy and Japanese legislation.
subfiles.summary: The proposed statement says FEC-045/5 leaves its precise application to SCAP and that the recent Japanese legislation is not inconsistent with the policy decision.

subfiles.title: Labor-Management Conference in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports on a SCAP-sponsored labor-management conference and its wage stabilization resolution.
subfiles.summary: Sebald describes SCAP’s effort to secure voluntary settlement of disputes and a no-strike pledge. Delegates disagreed over dispute machinery, while a committee endorsed linking wage increases to productivity.

subfiles.title: Labor Situation in Japan, Korea and Okinawa
subfiles.about: Records Assistant Secretary of Labor Gibson’s observations after visiting Japan, Korea, and Okinawa.
subfiles.summary: Gibson criticizes the sharp shift in Japanese occupation labor policy and recommends American union advisers, education, and changes to the National Public Service Law. He also discusses inefficient coal industries in Japan and Korea, weak Korean unions, and low Army wages for Okinawan workers.

subfiles.title: Visit of Assistant Secretary of Labor Gibson to Japan
subfiles.about: Records Gibson’s discussion with State and Labor officers about his Japan visit and proposed labor measures.
subfiles.summary: Gibson urges a U.S. trade union mission, changes to public service penalties and the 48-hour week, and treatment of communications workers like railway and monopoly employees. He says MacArthur promised Washington a chance to review proposed labor legislation.

subfiles.title: Recent Developments in the Japanese Labor Situation
subfiles.about: Records Gibson’s assessment of Communist influence and proposed reforms to Japanese labor policy.
subfiles.summary: Gibson links Communist gains partly to the 48-hour government work week and restrictive public service law. He recommends revising that law, appointing moderate unionists to mediation bodies, establishing a minimum wage, supporting the Democratization League, and exchanging American and Japanese labor leaders.

subfiles.title: Recent Developments in the Japanese Labor Situation
subfiles.about: Provides a second copy of the March 1 record of Gibson’s Japanese labor briefing.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Gibson’s concerns about Communist influence and the National Public Service Law, plus his recommendations for labor exchanges, a minimum wage, moderate representation, and democratic union procedures.

subfiles.title: Australian FEC Proposal on Japanese Government Enterprise Workers
subfiles.about: Discusses an Australian proposal to apply FEC trade union policy to workers in Japanese government enterprises.
subfiles.summary: Bishop reports support for the proposal among FEC members and recommends frank discussions with friendly delegations. He argues that detailed implementation should remain with SCAP and Japan, while the United States supports trade union development without weakening SCAP’s authority.

subfiles.title: Reply Concerning Gibson’s Report on Labor in Japan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Tobin’s letter and Gibson’s report on Japanese labor.
subfiles.summary: The draft says Under Secretary Webb will handle Gibson’s recommendations for the Department.

subfiles.title: Possible U.S. Labor Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Records discussion of MacArthur’s and Dodge’s objections to an official American labor mission.
subfiles.summary: Gibson presses for a mission to counter Communist influence; Voorhees proposes consultations with Tobin and possibly taking labor advisers on his own Japan trip.
